content: The term helipad is a portmanteau derived from helicopter landing pad, referring to a designated area specifically designed for helicopter landings. While helicopters are capable of landing on any flat surface, a purpose-built helipad provides a clearly marked, hard surface that is free from obstacles, ensuring a safe landing zone. Helipads are typically constructed from concrete and are marked with a circle and/or the letter H to make them easily identifiable from the air. They are often located at heliports or airports, where additional facilities such as fuel, air traffic control, and aircraft servicing are available. However, unlike heliports, helipads generally do not offer full-time air traffic control or fueling and maintenance services. Helipads can also be situated in remote or unconventional locations. For instance, they are frequently installed on the rooftops of hospitals to facilitate medical evacuations (commonly referred to as MEDEVACs). Large ships may also feature helipads to accommodate helicopter landings, and some businesses maintain helipads on the roofs of their office buildings for corporate use. While concrete is the most common material for helipad construction, temporary helipads can be built from wood in remote areas, such as those used by forest firefighters to receive supplies. In extreme conditions, helipads may even be constructed on frozen ice to support operations in challenging environments. The highest helipad in the world, built by India, is located on the Siachen Glacier at an altitude of 21,000 feet above sea level. Rooftop helipads often display a large two-digit number, which indicates the weight limit of the pad in thousands of pounds. Additionally, retractable helipad systems have been developed as an innovative solution to address significant challenges in the helicopter travel industry. These systems provide a flexible and efficient landing surface, adapting to specific operational needs.
